paper_title: VibeVideoAgent: Closing the Perceptual Loop for Code-Driven Video Generation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Code-driven video generation asks a coding agent to write and run rendering programs. This gives exact control over typography, data visualizations, synchronized audio, and multi-shot scenes, and it leaves an editable project behind. A program that exits cleanly can still render overlapping labels, a camera aimed away from its subject, broken object interactions, or narration that drifts out of sync, and none of these raise a runtime error. Feeding rendered frames and audio back into the coding session bloats its long-horizon context, while critiquing only the finished full-resolution render turns early design mistakes into costly rewrites. We introduce VibeVideoAgent, a training-free framework that lets coding agents inspect their drafts throughout production. Multimodal perception runs in short-lived contexts kept apart from the coder and returns compact, grounded Findings. Seven primitives operate on a unified multi-clock representation of assets and drafts: they explore media from coarse to fine, verify quoted requirements with evidence from every required modality, compare a draft with a reference or an earlier revision on separate clocks, and measure stream signals locally. A lightweight staged protocol has the agent test its riskiest decision on a minimal preview first. On all 239 VibeVideoBench tasks, with matched agent runtimes and a fixed perception model, VibeVideoAgent improves holistic audiovisual quality (L3) for Claude Opus 5.5 (4.03 -> 4.43, while L2 rubric compliance rises from 98.87% to 99.35%), GPT-6 Astra (4.03 -> 4.27), and Claude Sonnet 5.5 (3.97 -> 4.10), with the largest gains in audio-visual synchronization (up to +0.56). Controlled ablations show that each component contributes, and trajectory audits show that the granularity of code edits governs the trade-off between rubric adherence and perceptual quality.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Pixel-space video generators [20, 31, 39, 52] and agentic pipelines built on them [46] produce compelling textures and motion, but they offer little control when creator needs exact typography, faithful mathematical or data charts, strict multi-shot continuity, precise audiovisual synchronization, or fine-grained edits afterward. Code-driven video generation, often called Vibe Video [6, 8, 10], treats video creation as programming instead. Given natural-language brief and raw assets, coding agent writes and runs rendering software (HTML/Canvas, React/Remotion, Cairo, Manim, FFmpeg audio pipelines, or Blender Python) that yields both playable video and an editable source project. Because every visual element, camera curve, and audio cue is defined in code, the approach covers both 2D audiovisual motion design [10, 58] and 4D cinematic previsualization [8, 40]. Coding agents write such programs fluently, yet they often fail at authoring video. In software engineering [49], defects usually surface as compiler errors or failing tests. Video authoring has three problems that such feedback does not reach (Figure 1a). First, successful run says little about what the viewer sees. script can exit with code zero and write valid MP4 in which character holds backpack in hand instead of wearing it, 3D camera orbits away from the protagonist, labels collide, or narration lags two seconds behind the chart it explains. Second, showing raw media to the coder pollutes its context. Production involves reference footage, design stills, partial shot previews, and several rough cuts, and appending their frames and audio to the agents history grows the context with every render and degrades long-horizon code maintenance [23, 26]. Third, critique at the end of the pipeline comes too late and cannot follow changes across versions. When only the finished full-resolution render is reviewed, Equal contribution. Corresponding author: Bin Wen. 1 VibeVideoAgent: Closing the Perceptual Loop for Code-Driven Video Generation Figure 1. Closing the perceptual loop in code-driven video generation. (a) conventional coding agent either ships unchecked renders, so visual, spatial, and sync bugs survive clean exit code, or puts raw frames and audio into its context 𝐶𝑡 and critiques only the final video, which leads to whole-project rewrites. (b) VibeVideoAgent keeps raw media out of 𝐶𝑡 : stateless VLM worker Φ and local probes Ψ return compact, grounded Findings 𝑓𝑡 at every stage, from minimal preview to final delivery. basic error in layout, rigging, or timing forces rewrite of the whole project. Code edits also shift cut timings, so re-inspecting single clip can accept an unverified fix or miss regression in neighboring shot. We address these problems with VibeVideoAgent, training-free framework that gives coding agents perceptual feedback while they produce video (Figure 1b). The coder never receives raw media. Dense audiovisual observation is delegated to short-lived perception calls, which return compact Findings grounded in space and time. This decoupling follows VideoNexus [26], which keeps video perception outside planners context when answering questions about fixed video. Authoring adds drafts that change with every edit and live on several clocks, requirements that span audio and vision, and repairs whose effect must be checked across versions. unified multi-clock draft representation addresses read-only reference assets, zero-duration design stills, shot previews placed at an offset in the film, and full cuts in the same way, and binds each observation to hashes of the source code behind it. On top of it, seven primitives serve four roles: (i) coarse-to-fine exploration of assets and drafts (describe_media, locate_event, inspect_segment, transcribe_speech); (ii) verification of requirements quoted from the brief, with deterministic check that the evidence covers every required modality (check_requirement); (iii) comparison of two media on separate clocks, against reference or across revisions to confirm repair (compare_media); and (iv) local probes of decoding, loudness, silence, frozen frames, and loop seams that need no API call (probe_media). lightweight staged protocol (plan_production) links quoted constraints in the brief to ordered production beats before any code is written, and has the agent test its riskiest decision on minimal preview before moving on to assembly, targeted repair, and delivery. Because the primitives operate on standard image, audio, and video containers, VibeVideoAgent needs no adapters for particular rendering engines: the same seven primitives serve 3D WebGPU/Canvas scenes, React/Remotion interfaces, Cairo and Manim graphics, SVG game simulations, and multi-track TTS/FFmpeg audio (Appendix D). We expose them through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) [2] to the native agentic coding CLIs, Claude Code and Codex CLI, with Gemini 3.8 Flash as fixed perception model, and compare each coding model (Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, and GPT-6 Astra) with its own native agent on all 239 VibeVideoBench tasks. Our contributions are: perceptual framework for in-production video authoring. training-free architecture that keeps dense audiovisual inspection out of the long-horizon coding context, so that agents can check early previews and repair their programs iteratively across heterogeneous rendering pipelines without engine-specific adapters. Multi-clock perception and verification primitives. unified multi-clock draft representation and seven primitives for coarse-to-fine exploration, modality-gated requirement checks, comparison with references and earlier revisions on separate clocks, and local signal probes, used under lightweight staged production protocol. Evaluation with three coding models. On all 239 tasks, VibeVideoAgent improves L3 over each native agent: +0.40 for Claude Opus 5.5 (with 99.35% L2), +0.24 for GPT-6 Astra (with 99.51% L1), and +0.13 for Claude Sonnet 5.5. Ablations and trajectory telemetry isolate each component and show how the frequency of verification and the granularity of edits shape the balance between L2 and L3. 2 VibeVideoAgent: Closing the Perceptual Loop for Code-Driven Video Generation

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Code-driven visual and video generation. Visual programming showed that language models can compose vision modules through executable code [14, 37]. Code generation now produces charts and plots [47, 51], web pages and interactive artifacts [35, 55, 58], and animations [24, 38], and MoVer [28] verifies generated motion graphics against logical specifications of their motion. For video, TheoremExplainAgent [21] and Code2Video [6] render educational Manim videos with storyboarding and layout critique, Paper2Video [59] and PresentAgent [33] turn documents into narrated presentations, Lab2Sim [15] turns experiment footage into simulation code, and WavJourney [25] composes audio from LLM-written scripts. SenseNova 6.8 Code2Video [32] is an open-weight model that renders short videos from the code it writes, OpenMotion [30] has coding agents rebuild reference videos as editable HTML, and VibeVideoBench [10] benchmarks the task in 12 categories. Most of these systems are tied to one medium or engine, whereas VibeVideoAgent offers one perceptual interface across graphics libraries, browsers, simulation loops, and multi-track audio. Agentic 3D scene synthesis and previsualization. Code also gives explicit control over 3D geometry, layout, and camera [11, 36, 50]. Several 3D systems check rendered views with VLM, for critique [17], edit search [18], visual question answering on CAD objects [1], or multi-agent refinement [27], but they look at still renders of single program state. CineRecon [40] and VibePrevisBench [8] evaluate multi-shot 4D reconstruction and previsualization, and find that agents fail when they cannot reconcile scene logic in code with what appears on screen. VibeVideoAgent addresses this screen-space gap over time, with reference-to-draft comparison, preview checks, and verification across revisions, and without engine-specific scene-graph extractors. Feedback-driven agents. Agents improve their outputs through self-refinement and reflection [29, 34], execution feedback on code [5, 43], and agentcomputer interfaces [44, 49, 53]. With visual feedback, Visual Sketchpad [16] lets multimodal models inspect their own sketches, Vision-as-a-Tool [48] gives coding agents inspection tools for static HTML, SVG, and 3D assets, and PhysLoop [7] refines pixel-space video generators with physics-simulation feedback. Generated video is usually scored after the fact, by benchmark suites [19] or multimodal LLM judges [3]; VibeVideoAgent instead uses multimodal model during production, on bounded excerpts and under deterministic validation. Agentic video understanding. For long videos [9, 13, 41], agents decide where to look: they compose models through language [54], retrieve frames or query memory [12, 42], search images for small details [45], or search long videos with tools [22, 57]. Sprout [4] replaces accumulated video inputs with textual memory tree built while answering, and VideoACE [56] tests whether agents adapt temporal coverage, sampling density, and spatial detail to fast actions. Our work builds on VideoNexus [26], which showed that planner can direct perception run in independent contexts and reason over compact, temporally grounded reports, with no visual tokens in its own context. These methods answer questions about fixed, finished video. Authoring is different: the media are mutable, incomplete, and spread over source, preview, and film clocks; claims often span audio and vision; and each code edit shifts event timing. VibeVideoAgent therefore adds multi-clock addressing, modality-gated verification, comparison across revisions on separate clocks, and deterministic signal probes.

sections.title: 3.3 Seven Perception and Verification Primitives
sections.content: Instead of one open-ended prompt that asks VLM about the video, VibeVideoAgent provides seven primitives, independent of the rendering stack and organized around four questions an author faces during production (Figure 2b; Appendix lists verdict sets and defaults). I. What is in my assets or current draft? Dense uniform sampling wastes budget and single sparse pass misses short transitions, so exploration proceeds from coarse to fine. describe_media returns 1 fps index of scenes, text, and sounds (or the layout of still) and is told not to treat an event missed at sparse sampling as absent. locate_event searches for queried object, action, or sound; on sparse scans ( 𝑓eff < 8 fps) it automatically re-queries up to two candidate windows at 8 fps to pin down onsets and cuts. inspect_segment answers diagnostic question about chosen window or pixel crop at 4 fps and can return up to six evidence frames to the coder. transcribe_speech uploads only the audio and returns timestamped verbatim utterances for cutting dialogue or aligning animation with narration. Open-ended VLM critiques tend to comment on aesthetics nobody asked about and to overlook subtle constraints, especially on cross-modal timing. check_requirement instead tests one explicit observable claim (2 fps by default) together with its quoted source and required modalities Mreq {visual, audio}. sections.title: 3.4 Staged Production Protocol
sections.content: Good perception tools answer how to inspect media but not when. Left alone, an agent may write an entire multi-minute project before its first check, or never check its riskiest requirement. VibeVideoAgent therefore pairs the primitives with lightweight staged protocol built around one local planning ledger (Figure 2c). Stage 0: plan gate (plan_production). After reading the brief and listing inputs/, and before any code edit, render, or media call (a pre-tool runtime gate enforces this), the agent records plan (G, D, Q, Bbeats, Cchoice, 𝑟first, 𝑝min). Each requirement 𝑟 must quote the brief verbatim (checked programmatically against B), state its observable phenomenon and required modalities, and link to at least one ordered beat in Bbeats. This separates what the user asked for from the creative choices Cchoice left to the agent. The agent also names the highest-risk requirement 𝑟first, whose failure would force the most rework, and the smallest render 𝑝min that can test it. In the minimal preview stage (stage=preview), the agent Stages 14: preview, assembly, repair, delivery. explores unfamiliar assets, renders 𝑝min (a still for typography or character design, short clip for motion or camera, or an audiovisual slice for narration sync), and checks 𝑟first before building the remaining beats. In rough-cut assembly (stage=assembly), it verifies cross-shot properties such as ordering, transitions, caption legibility, and speech-to-graphic sync on cheap rough cuts. In targeted repair (stage=revision), an uncertain verdict leads the agent to refine the window, frame rate, crop, or modality instead of guessing an edit, and fail verdict shows where to patch; the agent then re-renders the affected slice and calls compare_media(finding_id, media) to confirm resolved and check the shifted neighbors. In verified delivery (stage=final), it runs probe_media on the encoded MP4, re-verifies requirements that compositing or mixing could break, registers the immutable output with its source files and replayable render command, and submits.

Agents receive natural-language brief and read-only assets, cannot call pixel-generation APIs, and must write rendering software that delivers playable MP4 and an editable source repository. Two official multimodal judges, Gemini 3.8 Flash and Gemini 4 Argon, score every delivery. Controlled single-variable comparison. Each coding model runs in its native CLI: Claude Code (claude -p, effort max) for Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5, and Codex CLI for GPT-6 Astra. All runs use isolated 16-vCPU Linux namespaces with identical rendering libraries and read-only inputs (0444). Every + VibeVideoAgent run registers the same MCP server and PreToolUse hook that blocks direct reads of raw media, sub-agents, and ad-hoc external API calls, so all perception goes through the seven audited primitives; wall time, provider tokens, and retries are logged. The perception model is fixed to Gemini 3.8 Flash (gemini-3.8-flash). Each + VibeVideoAgent delivery is paired with the models official Native Agent baseline on the same task, and component ablations use Claude Opus 5.5 on 36-task diagnostic subset (Section 4.3). Hidden rubrics and judges stay outside the authoring filesystem and run only after the output MP4 and source snapshot are frozen by SHA-256.

sections.title: 4.2 Main Results
sections.content: VibeVideoAgent improves every coding model. VibeVideoAgent raises the dual-judge L3 Mean of all three models  (Table 1)  , by 0.40 for Claude Opus 5.5, 0.24 for GPT-6 Astra, and 0.13 for Claude Sonnet 5.5. (i) The largest gains are temporal and cross-modal. AQ improves the most for every model (+0.56 for Opus, +0.40 for Sonnet, +0.32 for Astra), followed by TM and CL. Native agents often write valid FFmpeg or TTS pipelines whose narration drifts behind transitions, is cut off at shot boundaries, or leaves dead air; modality-gated check_requirement, transcribe_speech, and probe_media expose these failures while the video is still in production. (ii) The gains are not tied to one judge. Gemini 3.8 Flash is both the perception model and one of the judges. Under this judge, L3 rises from 4.14 to 4.60 for Opus (124 task wins, 11 losses), from 4.10 to 4.43 for Sonnet, and from 4.11 to 4.59 for Astra (121 wins, 16 losses). Under the independent and stricter Argon judge, Opus still gains 0.80 pp L2 (98.36% 99.15%) and 0.33 L3 (3.91 4.25; 132 wins, 37 losses), and Astra raises L2 from 98.38% to 99.00%. (iii) The interface transfers across CLI runtimes. With VibeVideoAgent, Opus reaches the highest L2 and L3 in Table 1 (4.374.46 on all five dimensions) and Astra the highest L1, so the same MCP interface works in both Claude Code and Codex CLI. Verification frequency and edit granularity. The telemetry in Table 2 reveals three distinct behaviors. Claude Opus 5.5 checks selectively and makes small patches (+0.48 pp L2, +0.40 L3). It edits after 77.4% (171/221) of failed checks and resolves 58.3% (88/151) of dual-clock rechecks with the least coding output of the three models. It makes 50.6 worker calls per task and has the highest dual-clock resolution rate (65.6%, 419/639); its output tokens are spread over 7.0 versions ( 25.7k each) as local diffs that fix missed rubric items and leave working code alone. sections.title: 4.3 Ablations and In-Production Analysis
sections.content: Treatment-blind diagnostic subset. More than 80% of tasks already reach 100% L2 with Native Opus 5.5, so random subset leaves little room to separate variants, while selecting tasks by the gains of VibeVideoAgent would bias the comparison through selection and regression to the mean. We therefore build deterministic subset of 36 tasks (15% of the benchmark) from native-baseline diagnostics and public task metadata alone, before running any ablation. Its four strata cover rubric bottlenecks (12 tasks), reference-grounded assets (8), audiovisual and temporal bottlenecks (10), and median-baseline guardrails (6); see Appendix F. Component ablations. The full system has the best L2 (3.44 pp above Native; 94.28% 99.11% under Argon) and the best score on every L3 dimension (+0.56 L3 Mean; Table 3), and each ablation hurts different aspect of the output. Without check_requirement, rubric precision and coherence suffer most: L2 drops by 1.15 pp (1.73 pp under Argon), and CL and VA each fall by 0.15. Ad-hoc inspection without quoted claims and required audio and visual evidence misses subtle constraints and accepts guesses from single modality. Without compare_media, repairs and timing suffer: L3 falls to 4.30, with the largest drops on VQ, TM, and AQ. The share of failed checks followed by an edit drops from 94.0% (47/50) to 78.3% (65/83), and motion fixes, reference mismatches, and audio shifts introduced by edits go unverified. Without probe_media, playability suffers: L1 drops the most (2.62 pp), and L3 falls by 0.16 under Argon, because sparse frame sampling cannot replace exact decoding, LUFS loudness, 50 dB silence, and frozen-frame analysis. Without the staged protocol (Tools-Only, which keeps all seven primitives but drops plan_production and the preview gate), L2 falls by 0.47 pp (1.05 pp under Argon) and L3 to 4.32. Preview-gate adherence drops from 97.2% to 0.0%, and dual-clock resolution falls from 70.6% (24/34) to 52.2% (12/23), as untested layout and rigging choices turn into expensive late rewrites. Context decoupling. Per task, perception workers process 386 frames and 171 of audio for Opus 5.5, 303 frames and 138 (75.2k prompt tokens) for Sonnet 5.5, and 1,297 frames and 660 (335.0k prompt tokens) for GPT-6 Astra, all outside the coding session, while the Findings stored in state.json average only 0.3k1.4k tokens. Replaying the same media through coding history of 3050 turns would cost tens of millions of input tokens per task. On an eight-task suite with exact single-turn response sizes (Appendix G), the returned Findings are 6.5 smaller than the perceived media (12.0 on the long-form explainer PA02), and L2 rises from 90.2% to 96.0% (Flash) and from 85.0% to 94.5% (Argon). Qualitative trajectory. Appendix (Figures 3 and 4) walks through recorded run on W0448. The agent finds three staging bugs in render that exited cleanly, confirms both patches with dual-clock compare_media, and returns uncertain where evidence is incomplete; Flash-judged L2 rises from 76.0% to 96.0%.

sections.title: 5 Limitations
sections.content: Perception samples bounded frame rates ( 16 fps) and selected intervals, so sub-frame glitches or windows that were never inspected can go unnoticed, even with 8 fps refinement and full-stream decoding. VibeVideoAgent 8 VibeVideoAgent: Closing the Perceptual Loop for Code-Driven Video Generation reports unobserved spans and missing modalities as uncertain, and the delivery check certifies that the file plays correctly; it does not certify the absence of semantic defects. Comparing hash-bound clips from before and after an edit shows that rendered symptom changed after declared edit. This is an observation and not causal proof over program branches: an edit to shared animation helper can affect beats that were never inspected if the agent skips neighbor checks. Finally, the external perception model (Gemini 3.8 Flash) can misread dense overlapping text or fine 3D depth ordering unless the agent requests crop or evidence frames, intermediate renders add compute and latency, and the behavior of commercial APIs may change with provider updates.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: Code-driven video generation gives agents precise control over layout, motion, sound, and camera, provided they can see and check what their code renders. VibeVideoAgent provides this feedback without filling the coding context with media: multi-clock media specification and seven primitives, used under lightweight staged protocol, let the agent catch defects early and verify its repairs across heterogeneous rendering stacks. On all 239 VibeVideoBench tasks, it improves holistic audiovisual quality for three frontier coding models (up to +0.40 L3 and +0.56 on AV sync) while raw media stay outside the coding session, and when the agent edits locally, rubric adherence and perceptual quality improve together. Future work includes guidance on edit locality for smaller coding models, adaptive scheduling of preview fidelity, open-weight perception models, and dedicated engines for 4D previsualization [8].

sections.title: C Deterministic Finding Validation Rules
sections.content: Every structured JSON response from the perception worker (media_worker.py) must conform to the schema {summary, verdict, evidence} and pass five controller-enforced checks before entering state.json: 14 VibeVideoAgent: Closing the Perceptual Loop for Code-Driven Video Generation 1. Excerpt index bounds. Each evidence rows media_index must reference valid input excerpt (0 for single-media calls; {0, 1} for compare_media). 2. Temporal and modality containment. Evidence times must satisfy 0 start end duration + 103 on the referenced excerpts clock, and modality {visual, audio} must be compatible with the excerpts extracted tracks. 3. Normalized box validity. Non-empty boxes are permitted only on visual evidence and must satisfy 0 𝑥1 < 𝑥2 1 and 0 𝑦1 < 𝑦2 1. 4. Cross-excerpt and cross-modality completeness. If any supplied excerpt receives no evidence rows, or any modality in required_evidence lacks cited evidence row on an excerpt, the verdict is deterministically downgraded to uncertain. 5. Comparison-mode and byte-identity guards. Reference-mode compare_media cannot emit revision verdicts (resolved/persists); revision-mode compare_media emitting resolved when SHA256(𝐸 src ) = 0 SHA256(𝐸 src 1 ) is downgraded to unchanged. Production Workflow Guidance and Cross-Stack Generality General production workflow policy. In VibeVideoAgent runs, the system prompt is extended with short five-step guidance: (1) read prompt.txt, task.json, and the input inventory, then call plan_production to separate quoted requirements from creative choices and select the smallest render capable of testing the highest-risk decision; (2) resolve unfamiliar input assets via describe_media, locate_event, transcribe_speech, or inspect_segment; (3) render the minimal preview early and verify first_requirement at stage=preview before scaling to the remaining beats; (4) assemble the remaining beats, inspect cut boundaries and AV synchronization at stage=assembly, and verify code repairs via compare_media(finding_id, media); and (5) run probe_media and stage=final checks on the exact encoded delivery file before calling register_artifact and submit_delivery. Zero-adapter operation across heterogeneous rendering pipelines. All primitives operate on standard images, audio streams, and video containers, and provenance can be bound to any source file, so no engine-specific adapters are needed: the seven MCP tool schemas and validation rules stay the same whichever rendering stack the coding agent chooses for brief. (1) In headless-browser and interactive 3D WebGPU/Canvas pipelines (Playwright, HTML/CSS, Three.js, React/Remotion), minimal previews capture single DOM or viewport stills or short framestepped clips to check layout legibility, 3D cutaway framing, and CSS/Canvas easing before full capture. (2) In Python vector, scientific, and game-simulation pipelines (Cairo, Pillow, SVG, Manim), early previews check coordinate geometry, mathematical notation, and sprite state transitions, and compare_media(reference, focus) aligns drafts with supplied reference visuals or motion specifications. (3) In narrated and music-driven pipelines (edge-tts, SciPy synthesis, FFmpeg filtergraphs), transcribe_speech, audiovisual check_requirement, and probe_media(loudness, silence) enforce speech-to-graphic timing and clean audio mixing without engine-specific plugins. Runtime Isolation and Post-Freeze Evaluation Each task executes in an isolated Linux user, mount, and PID namespace with its own CLI runtime configuration directory (Claude Code for Claude models; Codex CLI for GPT-6 Astra) and locked MCP settings. The perception_gate.py hook intercepts every PreToolUse event, logs its decision to perception_gate.jsonl, and denies (i) direct Read calls on binary image, audio, video, or PDF files; (ii) sub-agent or alternative MCP invocations; (iii) writes outside workspace/ or inside the read-only workspace/inputs/; and (iv) shell commands that attempt to invoke external model endpoints or inspect API credentials. Official benchmark rubrics and VLM or scene judges reside outside the task filesystem and are executed only after run.json reaches terminal state and the delivered MP4 hash is frozen. 15 VibeVideoAgent: Closing the Perceptual Loop for Code-Driven Video Generation

sections.title: F Ablation Subset Construction
sections.content: More than 80% of the benchmark tasks already reach 100% L2 under Native Opus 5.5, so uniform random sampling squeezes the differences between variants against the ceiling, while selecting tasks by the gains of + VibeVideoAgent would introduce post-hoc selection and regression-to-the-mean bias. We therefore build deterministic, treatmentblind, capability-stratified subset of 36 tasks (15% of VibeVideoBench) only from native-baseline diagnostics and public task metadata, before running any ablation. It has four strata: Rubric-bottleneck stratum (12 tasks): multi-constraint briefs with Native L2 < 98.0%, stressing upfront requirement decomposition and sourced contract verification. Reference-grounded asset stratum (8 tasks): tasks supplying external video, image, or audio assets in inputs/ (sorted by lowest Native L3), directly exercising coarse-to-fine asset exploration and reference-mode compare_media. Audiovisual and temporal bottleneck stratum (10 tasks): audio-mandated tasks with the lowest baseline L3 and AQ scores, stressing modality-gated check_requirement, transcribe_speech, and probe_media. Median-baseline guardrail stratum (6 tasks): standard tasks across major categories (D, W, ZH) with Native L2 = 100% and median Native L3 4.00, verifying that closed-loop inspection does not over-edit already compliant drafts. sections.title: H Recorded Production Trajectory
sections.content: Figure 3 traces one complete recorded run of VibeVideoAgent (Claude Opus 5.5) on VibeVideoBench task W0448. The task asks for 20.0 (19201080, 30 fps) wordless life story in six stages (Childhood, Youth, 95, Family, Aging, Farewell), anchored by recurring red button (#D94C3A) that opens and closes the film as seamless loop. Before any rendering code is written, plan_production extracts 13 verbatim-quoted requirements across 7 beats and marks multi-age character identity (R_identity) as the highest-risk decision. The agent tests it first on single rendered lineup still (previews/lineup.png) with check_requirement(stage=preview), which returns pass (box [0.07, 0.44, 0.55, 0.82]). The agent then scales the verified rig to the first 600-frame film v1.mp4, which passes the opening, office, and aging checks, but assembly-stage checks return three fail verdicts. In Youth ([4.18, 5.05] s, box [0.69, 0.48, 0.81, 0.82]), the protagonist catches the backpack and holds it down in hand instead of slinging it onto the shoulder. In Family ([9.90, 11.65] s), no laptop lid closes before the character stands ([9.90, 10.65] s), and child is already waiting inside the doorway instead of running in from off-screen ([10.90, 11.65] s). In Farewell ([17.38, 19.00] s), the coat hangs on stand beside the empty chair. This fails the stricter observable that the agent wrote itself (draped on it) but satisfies the verbatim prompt_quote (Beside an empty chair, place Ps coat). Because check_requirement keeps both strings, the agent keeps the Farewell staging that follows the prompt (and notes this in submit_delivery.notes). It patches project/render.py for the three real bugs in Youth and Family, renders v2.mp4, and calls compare_media with the earlier Finding IDs. Both dual-clock rechecks return resolved against the archived v1 excerpts ([4.68, 6.18] for R_youth; [9.90, 10.40] and [11.15, 11.65] for R_family). The agent then checks R_end_zoom at stage=final on the closing excerpt [18.50, 20.00] alone, after an earlier call on [18.60, 20.00] was rejected by the deterministic post-validator. check_requirement confirms the zoom into red ([19.13, 19.88] s) but returns uncertain instead of guessing pass, because the opening zoom-out lies outside that window. probe_media(decode) passes, and local RGB seam check confirms the loop. The run uses 13 perception-worker calls (412 frames, 12 accepted Findings), with 32,079 prompt tokens for accepted Findings (32,320 in total) against 5,811 serialized Finding tokens and 4,561 model output tokens. Under the Gemini 3.8 Flash judge, it raises the task-rubric pass rate from 76.0% (19/25) for the native Opus 5.5 baseline to 96.0% (24/25), with Content Logic rising from 3 to 5 and Timing & Motion from 3 to 4. Figure 4 shows the same run with real frames, together with three other tasks that use the same seven primitives on different rendering stacks. Figure 3. Recorded production trajectory on W0448 (a 20.0 s, 19201080, 30 fps six-stage life-story loop). Every timestamp, normalized box, and verdict is copied from state.json; Finding spans are drawn on 020 film ruler. The agent validates the cross-age character design on one preview still and catches three silent staging bugs in R_youth and R_family in v1.mp4. It also separates an over-specific observable it wrote for R_farewell (marked fail*) from the satisfied prompt_quote. It then patches render.py, confirms both repairs with dual-clock compare_media, and finishes with decode and seam probes, leaving R_end_zoom as uncertain. The bottom row reports perception cost, context compression, and the Flash-judged outcome against the native Opus 5.5 baseline. 17 VibeVideoAgent: Closing the Perceptual Loop for Code-Driven Video Generation Figure 4. End-to-end authoring with VibeVideoAgent. (a) The recorded W0448 run with real frames. (1) plan_production decomposes the brief, and single stage=preview lineup still verifies cross-age character identity before full rendering. (2) stage=assembly checks catch silent staging bugs in v1.mp4 even though the render exited cleanly: the backpack is held in hand, and in the Family beat no lid closes while the child already stands in the doorway. (3) compare_media(finding_id, media) confirms targeted render.py patch across shifted clocks. (4) Deterministic probe_media checks finalize the seamless red-button loop. Raw frames stay inside short-lived Gemini 3.8 Flash calls, whose Findings are 5.5 smaller than the media they perceive. (b) Without engine-specific adapters, the same seven primitives serve an interactive 3D WebGPU system (W0154, +71.1 pp L2 under the Argon judge), long-form paper explainer with synchronized narration (PA02, 12.0 smaller payload), and reference-guided reconstruction of motion and audio (R0009, Flash-judged L3 3.60 4.80).
